Flake Out
FLAYK OWT
verb (Boomer slang)
From flake, a thin scale or chip (Webster 1828 has the noun of snow and other flakes), whence to flake off, to peel away. Mid-twentieth-century American slang used flake out for collapsing or falling asleep from exhaustion; baseball slang of the 1950s called an eccentric player a flake or flaky, and by the 1960s–70s flaky meant unreliable and to flake (out) meant to fail to show up or follow through. A flake is someone you cannot count on.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To flake out once meant to collapse from exhaustion; to Boomers and their children it mostly means to bail — to not show up, to forget, to drop a commitment at the last minute. "He said he’d help me move and then flaked." A flake is a person you cannot count on. The Christian observation: Scripture places reliability near the center of godly character, and it describes the flake vividly. "Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint" (Pro 25:19) — you lean on him at the worst moment and he gives way. The man who may dwell in God’s holy hill is the one who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psa 15:4) — he keeps his word even when it costs him. Our Lord asked for plain, dependable speech: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). His own disciples flaked on Him in His hour of need: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Mat 26:40). And He warned that discipleship admits no flaking: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luk 9:62). The comfort is that the Lord who was flaked on is Himself utterly faithful — He forgave Peter and restored him. A father teaches reliability best by being reliable: showing up to the game, keeping the promised fishing trip, being home when he said he would be.

Webster 1828 Definition

Mid-20th-c. slang (from flake, to peel away) for collapsing from exhaustion, and in Boomer and later usage for failing to show or follow through — the unfaithful man who is like a broken tooth in time of trouble (Pro 25:19).

FLAKE OUT, v.i. (American slang, mid-20th c.; Boomer era–present) 1. To collapse or fall asleep from exhaustion. 2. To fail to show up or keep a commitment; to back out. Flake, n., an unreliable or eccentric person; flaky, adj.

Webster (1828) — FLAKE, verb intransitive To break or separate in layers; to peel or scale off. We more usually say, to flake off.

Decode for families: "don’t be a flake" is one of the most useful sentences a parent can teach.

Key Scripture

Pro 25:19 — "Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint."

Psa 15:4 — "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

Mat 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Mat 26:40 — "And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour?"

Luk 9:62 — "And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."

Modern Corruption

Flaking treats commitments as provisional and one’s word as cheap; Scripture makes faithfulness to one’s word a mark of the man who dwells in God’s holy hill.

expand to see more

The 1970s celebrated spontaneity and distrusted commitment, and the word flake grew up in that soil. If you keep your options open and follow your feelings, you will flake; it is built in. The modern world has made it worse: a text message lets a person cancel at the last minute without facing anyone. The flake rarely thinks of himself as a liar, but Scripture treats an unkept word as a serious matter. The man of Psalm 15 keeps his oath even to his own hurt.

The deepest answer to flakiness is the faithfulness of God. "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." The disciples flaked in Gethsemane (Mat 26:40), and Christ did not flake on them; He went to the cross. A Christian who has been loved by a God who never backs out learns to keep his own word — to show up, to follow through, to finish the furrow (Luk 9:62).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old Norse flakna (to flake off) → English flake (a thin scale; 1828) → mid-20th-c. flake out (to collapse) → 1950s baseball flaky → 1960s–70s flake (unreliable person).

expand to see more

Old Norse flakna — to flake off, to split

English flake — a small loose piece, as of snow (see Flake)

Mid-20th c.: flake out — to collapse, to fall asleep

1950s baseball: flake, flaky — an eccentric player

1960s–70s: flaky — unreliable; to flake — to fail to show

Usage

""Grandpa has never flaked on a promise in his life. That’s why we believe him about the fish.""

"He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not (Psa 15:4)."

"Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth (Pro 25:19)."
